utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Igor Pantelic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is nothing that need delay us, may the usher please -- yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a quick information while the -- the witness is escorted. If, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, Mr. Pantelic, Mr. O'Sullivan, and myself, if we can be excused at -- well, in ten minutes from now because we have a meeting with the Office of the Prosecutor concerning the exhumations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, good afternoon to you, sir. You may resume your seat. Before I invite Mr. Krgovic to continue his cross-examination, I remind you, you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rodic, let us continue where we left off yesterday. My last question had to do with a document, so now I would like us to look at Exhibit P602. Mr. Rodic, this is the report that we looked at yesterday, and you also had an opportunity to look at it during your interview with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would like the witness to be shown page 3 of this document, in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, in the first paragraph here, we have a description of the premises in Keraterm, and it is said that these are -- this is the administration building with the restaurant, offices, halls, and the toilets and bathrooms. And you will agree with me that there is no mention of any bad conditions that you were able to observe here?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately, yes, that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like the witness to look at page 4 in the Serbian version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 2 here. You said that you spent a few days in Omarska too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A day or two at the beginning. I can't really recall, but it was in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 describes the conditions, and it says here that this is a relatively new facility which has all the necessary facilities for life and accommodation of a large number of persons: Offices, halls, toilets and washrooms, kitchen and dining-room, constant supply of drinking water, a large number of showers, constant supply of electricity. No alterations were made to the facility, but the existing premises were used for the accommodation of and work with the prisoners. And then it goes on to say there is no barbed wire around the facility, and it is quite a long way from the settlements of Omarska and Maricka. Basic health care was provided -- is provided for the prisoners in the investigation centre. Food is prepared in the Omarska iron/ore mine kitchen, and it is served in the centre restaurant on a self-service line. Mr. Rodic, having read this report, this part of the report, one could conclude that the conditions in Omarska were good?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, both facilities had been used before, and they were, indeed, relatively new. So this description of facts corresponds to the actual state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you don't know to what extent -- or, rather, which prisoners were allowed to use those premises and the conveniences listed here.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I don't know what and to what extent they were able and allowed to use here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, look at page 5 of this document. Please look at paragraph 3 here. In the Serbian version, that's the third paragraph from the top; and in the English version, that would be the first paragraph that we have here. It says here that of the total of persons brought into the investigation centre, two Muslims died of natural causes and 49 persons left the investigation centre in an unknown manner. Do you see this information?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to gather from this report, Keraterm is described as a transfer centre from which people were then transferred to Omarska or to Trnopolje or then further on to Manjaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards Keraterm, it is true, in a way. Quite a few people came in, a certain number of people were released while it was possible, and a certain number of people were then transferred on to Omarska and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this information about the number of people who died in the centre, it does not correspond to the truth?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot comment on this information because I was in the that area, so I don't really know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that this report does not contain any information about the killing of those persons in room number 3 that the Prosecutor asked you about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice anything of the sort in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, let us go back to page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, in paragraph 2 on this page, we have a description of Trnopolje. And here we see the description of the conditions there, and it is stated there that the open reception centre Trnopolje is located in the Trnopolje settlement, inhabited area, and it is used as an accommodation facility for the persons staying there. And these are the premises of the elementary school, the hall, the warehouse, and the private homes near those facilities as well as the open-air area in the yard. From the 24th of May, 1992, a relatively large number of citizens of Muslim ethnicity of both genders and all ages have sought refuge in the centre. Then we see the number of persons stated here. And then the report goes on to say the number of persons in this centre changes every day, and no special record are kept since the citizens are allowed to leave the camp as they see fit and to go wherever they like. Then in paragraph number 3 it is stated that there is a water supply, electricity supply in the camp, that the area is not fenced in, and that citizens are not interrogated in the centre. And the army personnel provides constant security for the facility, in case of any threats to the citizens from the outside by the extremists. And then it goes on to say that an outpatient clinic is there, that the representatives of the Red Cross are present. Mr. Rodic, you did not carry out any investigative actions or you didn't make any Official Notes regarding any of the persons in Trnopolje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We didn't go there. We didn't take any actions in Trnopolje. I did not stay in that area in that period. I am familiar with the location, and I know that the description is accurate. You have the school, the hall, the shops, and the private homes around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the area was fenced in?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do know is that there was a shop nearby, and the warehouse was fenced in, and the shop itself was actually in the warehouse. And that was the only part of the whole facility that was fenced in, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, do you know that, apart from this report, report by any -- by this commission, whether there were any other reports about the conditions in the collection centres?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any other efforts of this kind, and, in fact, the first time that I saw this report was in the course of the investigation, when it was shown to me by the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you and your colleagues from the state security or public security, when you made the Official Notes, when you did your job, you did not go into that, you did not send any reports further up about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not. We focussed in our reports or in our Official Notes, we focussed only on that, and this was the only form of communication that we had in that time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, in the team in Keraterm, was Djuro Savic there too?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know a man by the name of Djuro Savic, but he was never there. And there was no Djuro Savic in our -- in our office there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And while you were in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think -- in fact, I know that he was not there. But as I've already told you, I was there just two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was Sredoje Novic in the team with you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I said who worked in the teams on those jobs. Nobody else was there, not the persons that you've just mentioned or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in Omarska, while you were there, he was not there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, do you know that in Omarska, while you were there, or did you hear of any killings of the prisoners by the guards and that it was done on a wager for a crate of beer?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your interview, the Prosecutor showed you a number of documents signed by Milos. And as far as I can recall, you said that you were not familiar with those reports and that you were not aware of any group called Milos operating in your area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was shown those documents, but I didn't know anything about them, and I -- when -- I told the investigator that this was not the appropriate form that we used in our daily communication for those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were in Keraterm and in Omarska, you did not see Predrag Radulovic there, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. But, as I said, I was there for a very short time, and I didn't see anyone from the outside, so to speak, anyone from outside of Prijedor. I'm now talking about the people who were involved in the investigative measures taking place up there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel be kind enough to switch off the mike while the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Krgovic, the interpreters remind you to switch off your microphone while the witness is answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Rodic. So my question was: You never saw Mr. Radulovic in Keraterm either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, nobody else was involved in investigative measures, apart from us six who were working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you in examination-in-chief about anyone else coming to visit Keraterm from other areas, and in response, you said, if I understood you correctly, that one of the guards mentioned a delegation and that Stojan Zupljanin was there as well. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. But I also said that that was conveyed by one of the guards. Therefore, whether that was really the case or not, I cannot say. There was a delegation which stayed for a while there. And after that, we inquired with the guards and I think that one of them said that Mr. Stojan Zupljanin was there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you personally did not see Mr. Stojan Zupljanin. You didn't see any member of the delegation. It was only after a while that you heard that Mr. Zupljanin might have been in that delegation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a high-level delegation visited Prijedor and also paid a visit to Omarska in the summer of 1992 in which context the names of Mr. Brdjanin and some other people were mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a delegation paying a visit, but that probably happened a couple of days after their visit. Whether it happened in Prijedor or not, I cannot say with any degree of certainty. And I also heard on that occasion that Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Brdjanin were members of that high-level delegation. I can't remember who else was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And probably this visit by this delegation to Omarska created some kind of confusion in the sense that they visited Keraterm too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that there was some confusion. I cannot say whether it happened in my head or in the head of that man who told me that because I didn't see it, and I really can't say with any degree of certainty that Mr. Zupljanin was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, can you tell me approximately when was it when you returned, whether it was in early August or mid-August? When was it you returned to your regular job?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was sometime in mid-August or the latter half of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your office was in the public security station. Which floor was that; the third or the fourth?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were on the top floor, which was actually the second floor. But if you count the ground floor, then it would be the third floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was your office close to the conference room in the Prijedor SJB?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conference room was in an auxiliary building that you could reach through the yard. Therefore, it was not close to our offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about the office of Simo Drljaca? Where was his office located?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was located on the floor below and in the wing opposite to the wing where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, do you know who General Bogdan Subotic is?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of him, of Mr. Subotic, but I don't know which position he held at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you had never seen him and you had never heard of him coming to the Prijedor public security station?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And particularly in the course of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I ever saw Mr. Subotic in person, and that includes that period as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you surely never heard of Mr. Zupljanin, following the period when you returned to the station, coming to the public security station?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Mr. Zupljanin came in that period. I saw Mr. Zupljanin in Prijedor only much later, and I think that had to do with some assembly sessions taking part in -- taking place in Prijedor, and I saw him in that context. But I allow for a possibility that I might be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honours? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put only a few questions to you because my learned friend Krgovic and I agreed to focus our cross-examination on certain matters and that he would do the bulk of the job in his part of cross-examination. Therefore, I'm going only to tackle a number of issues that might require some clarification. Let me just remind you of a document that you discussed at length with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, that's P583. Can we just enlarge the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just refresh your memory. I'm not going to dwell long on this document. And this paragraph speaks about the categorisation of persons that the Prosecutor asked you about. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, my question is a question in principle. You were a member of a so-called mixed team made up of members of the State and Public Security Services, and you said yesterday that there were military personnel involved as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The essential purpose of your job was to establish who, among the people you interrogated, might have been involved or implicated in the commission of certain crimes and to what extent. Now, in short, was that your task? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that corresponds more or less to what we were doing. In these interviews, we tried to get as much information as possible about the persons who might have been involved in such activities or similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then you will certainly agree with me that the selection of suspects, according to the type of crime and the degree of involvement in the commission of certain crimes, was a lawful operative activity that all organs of the interior normally conduct all over the world, including our country. You would agree with me on that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that, according to the law in force at the time, those were the tasks that we were supposed to carry out during that pre-war and war period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to move to a different subject. In response to the questions put to you by the Prosecutor and my colleague Krgovic, you said that practically your methodology of work employed by members of the State and Public Security Services and your line of work was - let me put it this way - frozen at the time because you became a member of the team that operated according to the methodology that was employed by members of the Public Security Service; am I right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And as I said earlier, during that period, we did not have much communication with our first-instance superior, that is to say, Banja Luka. As for the latter part of your question, that was also true. That was only part of the activities that was any way part of the job description of members of the -- of the public security --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat whether he said "public" or "state" security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the interpreters ask that you repeat your last answer to counsel's question, notably whether you said "public security" or "state security." The interpreter did not catch that. So please if could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I said state security. That that was only part of the job that the state security had within its general job description.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, Mr. Rodic, during that period, you did not maintain any significant communication with your basic service in Banja Luka because, as I understand, the results of your work ended in the -- in the hands of Mr. Simo Drljaca, the chief of the Prijedor SJB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that we didn't have any communication whatsoever with Banja Luka, with the exception of the colleague who used to come to pay some kind of -- visit us as a kind of courtesy, and I know that all these reports ended up as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Speaking of that, I'm going to put a direct question to you: How many times during that period did you go to Banja Luka? And did you use any other communication channels to liaise with Banja Luka? And did you have any difficulties in that respect?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of April until the second half of September, I did not go to Banja Luka, nor do I remember any of my colleagues going there. We didn't have any other channels of communication. I think that even the telephone was broken or at least broken for the most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate answer to the question: When was it that you first heard who the interior minister of Republika Srpska was, and how did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from the media. And I cannot give you an approximate date. I think it was more or less at the time when it happened, but I really can't give you the time. I can't recall the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And for all intents and purposes, this was all the knowledge that you had about the existence of the minister of the interior; in other words, what you heard from the media?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I heard this in the media, and I may have heard something in that context regarding some activities or something like, but I did not have any personal first-hand knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, my colleague Mr. Krgovic showed you documents generated by the Crisis Staff indicating that it was the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality that actually established the collection centres or whatever we can call it. And I will show you a document but for another purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at 1D166. The document is a bit small. Can we please zoom in on the top part of the document. First two paragraphs. We won't be looking at the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, to confirm what Mr. Krgovic has already shown you, you can see in the heading of this document that in line with the decision of the Crisis Staff, in order to implement this decision, collection centres are set up. As can you see from paragraph 1, you will see that Mr. Simo Drljaca signed this document. We will look at page 2. So can you see in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And there's a reference to the decision of the Crisis Staff. That's the decision that you looked at yesterday with my colleague Mr. Krgovic. You do remember that Mr. Krgovic showed you this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can go through this document until we reach the last page, paragraph 15. I think that in the English version we need to go back one page. Yes, item number 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, I think you may have already read it, but let's go through it. Mr. Drljaca strictly prohibits any provision of any information whatsoever concerning the functioning of the collection centre, and all official documents must be kept at the collection centre and may be taken out or destroyed only with the permission of the chief of the Prijedor SJB. The security staff shall be responsible for this. Now, Mr. Rodic, in the context of your evidence and what you've just told me, if we establish a link with this order issued by Mr. Drljaca, it does appear that Mr. Drljaca, in fact, monopolized the right to gathering all information about all the events in the territory of the Prijedor municipality in a way by issuing this decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a bit of a misleading question because this document pertains to Omarska camp, and this witness was at Keraterm camp. So I don't know what link my learned friend is trying to draw here. Perhaps he wants to ask whether a similar order was issued with regard to Keraterm camp. That would probably be a feasible question this witness could answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the essence of my question does not pertain to the operation of any of the collection centres. It's the conduct, the behaviour, of Mr. Simo Drljaca regarding an embargo on the information in the Prijedor municipality, and I'm using it as a reference for further questions. So I'm not now dealing with Omarska or with Keraterm; I'm just trying to explore this issue with the witness. I haven't yet embarked on it. So may I be allowed to finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What I thought Mr. Olmsted's objection was going be is that the question, as phrased, invited an argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be quite specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, to the extent to which you came to know Mr. Drljaca, would you agree with me that he, as the chief of the SJB, was quite autonomous in his work, in relation to the rest of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and other responsible organs?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I guess -- I suppose if the witness can answer that, but it does call for speculation if this witness was in Prijedor during this time and did not go to other municipalities. And so how is he going to be able to compare what was happening in Prijedor with other places during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if the witness can give us any information, then, please, let him; and, if not, we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, you've read this order by Mr. Drljaca. Is that how he acted when it came to the information he received from you? Because you said that your information also went to him.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that information that we produced went to the MUP, to the SUP building, and this is the first time that I see this part of the document, where he actually issues an explicit order to that effect. As far as Mr. Drljaca is concerned, as a superior officer, I can't really say much because I did not have that much contact with him. And it was mostly common courtesy; we would meet on the staircase, things like that. But if -- I can tell you this: I did know him to a degree before the war from sports activities and recreation activities, where he always wanted to be the dominant figure. He was rather brazen, and I thought this was not acceptable for everyone. Now I cannot say whether he behaved in the same way in his work in this period because I don't know him all that well. He was not my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I will not dwell on that. Yesterday, Mr. Krgovic showed you a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Zecevic [sic] for the previous document, that is, 1D166, you said that the witness looked at it yesterday "with my colleague Mr. Krgovic. Do you remember that Mr. Krgovic showed you this document?" And the witness answers: "Yes, I do remember." I'm sorry, but I don't remember, and I don't see that in -- in the -- in the transcript. I don't think 166 has been showed. 167 has been showed. Just -- I don't know whether it's important, but this shows how easy one can mislead a witness, if I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, that was not my intention. And I didn't mean to say that this document was shown to him. That's not what I said. If you recall, I showed him just the heading, the letterhead of this document, or, rather, the preamble where the decision on -- of the Crisis Staff to establish those collection centres is referred to. Mr. Krgovic spoke about that and showed another document, and I just reminded the witness that he had discussed this topic with Mr. Krgovic, but not that this document was shown to him by Mr. Krgovic. And I fully agree with you. Mr. Krgovic did not show him this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just try and remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You remember that Mr. Krgovic showed you this decision on the release of persons from detention. It was a decision of the Crisis Staff. And you said that the Crisis Staff decided who would be released from those collection centres. Do you recall that? Do you recall having seen that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That misstates his evidence. He did not say that the Crisis Staff released persons. He said he didn't know. Can you maybe point to us where in the transcript he made that assertion, that the Crisis Staff decided who was released?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, well the gist of my question is merely to ask him whether he recalls discussing this topic with Mr. Krgovic and whether Mr. Krgovic actually showed him this document. I didn't want to comment on his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you remember that Mr. Krgovic showed you the decision to release some persons from the collection centres. Do you remember? And I can give you the reference. That's 1D167. And can you look at the document, if you wish, to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I consider this document as a follow-up on the document issued by the Crisis Staff, the one that was shown. I think this was yet another document that spoke about the establishment of detention centres or camps. And the previous document I considered to be the follow-up on the other one; in a way, Mr. Simo Drljaca's response to it, when he reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see the document that I mean on the screen. And do you remember having seen this document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Krgovic showed you this document, and you commented on this document. Let me now show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's P663.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will give you some time for you to read some parts of this document. Have you been able to read it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, if you look at this document really closely, Mr. Simo Drljaca - we will see the last page, and we will see that he signed it - is reporting to the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality on the implementations of the conclusions of the Crisis Staff. So let us look at the kind of conclusions we're talking about. Look at the conclusion that pertains to the procurement of uniforms for the police. I think it's the second conclusion.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we're now on page 2 and we need --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will now check what you're looking at, that we're now at page 2 so that you can see that Mr. Simo Drljaca signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, now you can see it. So you see the conclusion, number 1, Simo Drljaca reports to the Crisis Staff that the conclusion that the release of prisoners is prohibited is fully observed. You told us yesterday who was -- who had the right to decide on the fate of the prisoners. And you can see conclusion number 2, that the Crisis Staff is dealing even with the procurement of police uniforms. Mr. Rodic, let me just ask you: This is something that the state should be dealing with. The state should be in charge of procuring uniforms for the police; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, supplying the police and the army was always done not at the municipal level but at the level of the republic or of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And then you can look at the conclusion about the police staff payroll. I think that's conclusion number 5. You see this conclusion. It says LD. That would be the salary of the police staff -- force. Force.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Well, I wasn't able to see it because you gave me the wrong reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I think that your comment regarding the uniforms would apply also to the salaries. Salaries should be paid from -- by the state, not by the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it had been until the war broke out, and I think that the municipalities have nothing to do with it now. This is not done at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now look at the last paragraph on this page where Mr. Drljaca refers to an order of the Crisis Staff to establish an intervention platoon, a joint intervention platoon, that would also include members of the military police. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the last one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, that would be on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You see that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see. The one that pertains to the establishment of this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now my question is very brief: Were you aware of the existence of such a unit; and, if so, who had established it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see people from that unit from time to time, but I did not know who had established it and on whose orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps this is a good opportunity for me to show you the document on the establishment of this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, can we please have Exhibit P803.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, you can see the date. And it says the Crisis Staff. Can you please read the order that Mr. Drljaca had referred to in the previous document. Can you please have a look at it. Did you manage to read it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, to the extent that you are aware of, the establishment of special police units, according to the Law on Internal Affairs, is exclusively under the jurisdiction of the minister of the interior; is that right? Or, rather, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I agree with you. Usually it would be higher-level organs, i.e., the ministry, would take care of personnel issues, recruitment, provision of uniforms, and salaries, et cetera. So this was a whole series of jobs that should have done by the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But obviously in Prijedor this was done by the Crisis Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I see in front of me, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just show you one more document issued by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D00-0924.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you know about this? Did you know that it was the municipality who paid for and bought uniforms and created a platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't know exactly that these kind of decisions had been taken. I didn't know that. But I did notice that this unit had been established, but I don't know on whose orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, then the next obvious question is: What's the purpose of this line of questions? It concerns documents that are already admitted. What's the purpose of learning this witness things he doesn't know? Shouldn't you try to learn the Court things -- tell the Court things we don't know?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I am pursuing this line of questioning in an attempt to elicit from witness for -- what he perhaps know. But it turns out that the witness is not aware of search facts, and I cannot know in advance what he was or wasn't aware of. So the next document, I think, was not admitted into evidence. But I wanted to ask him about the blockade of the town that is mentioned in this document, and I wanted to ask him if he knew anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, have you read this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I don't know what was undertaken in this respect, but I know that there were check-points around the town on the main roads. But whether there were any activities involved, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was that felt, or did it affect the freedom of movement and the possibility for people to leave Prijedor? Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you anything about that because during that period, I moved very little around the town. And, besides, I don't know how these check-points operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, I have no further questions for you. I have finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, I want to return one more time to this delegation visit to Keraterm camp. How soon after this delegation visited Keraterm did the guard tell you that Mr. Zupljanin was part of that delegation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday that I wasn't able to pin-point the date. Therefore, I honestly cannot tell you how soon it happened after the visit. I don't know if it happened concurrently. I cannot tell you more than what I already told you, and that is what the guard told me. And I cannot make any further comments on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, you testified that you recall hearing sounds of cars coming that day and arriving at Keraterm. Is that what prompted you to go down and ask the guards what was going on, was there a delegation here, who was in it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can I have a reference when the witness said that about the car?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at transcript page 14499.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, unless I am wholly missing the thrust of your questions, it seems to me that you're on an impossible quest, if you're trying to establish the fact of -- of the -- who was present from this witness's testimony, because he's explained that he didn't know. He heard, and he heard this from the guards. And can -- can -- can you go -- can you take the witness further?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, the only place I want to go further is -- is when he had this conversation with the guards. And he's having trouble remembering that. And I'm trying to associate with him finding out that -- or hearing that a bunch of cars were coming and whether that's what prompted him to go speak to the guards about this event. If he can't answer it, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So, Mr. Rodic -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know if it makes a difference, but go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just very quickly, Mr. Rodic. You testified during the examination that you heard sounds of cars arriving that day. And my question to you: Is that what prompted you to go down and speak to the guards about this delegation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, it's leading. First you ask him: Did he go to ask guard or not. And when. If he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't believe it's leading, Your Honours. It's a question, whether him hearing these vehicles arriving that day, that's what prompted him to go and speak to the guards about this delegation that he has talked about, that he has testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Whether it is leading, Mr. Olmsted, I would have thought that you would have taken the hint from the Bench that whatever the answer is, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then I'm just going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, you testified during the examination that once you submitted your Official Notes from Keraterm to the typist, that was the last you saw of them. Today Mr. Cvijetic suggested to you that these Official Notes ended up in the hands of Simo Drljaca, and I think you may have agreed with that. Can you tell us, do you know whether, in fact, your Official Notes they were actually given to Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that the Official Notes were sent to the SUP. I didn't tell Mr. Cvijetic that it was Mr. Simo Drljaca who received them. I just said that they were sent to the SUP, and that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 1D166.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you'll recall this. A few minutes ago you were shown this by Mr. Cvijetic. This is an order regarding Omarska camp by the CS -- or the SJB chief from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could just turn to the last page of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, we can see that there are a list of seven organs to which copies of this order were submitted. And we see under number 3 the Security Service Centre in Banja Luka. Mr. Rodic, given the system of subordination that existed in 1992, was this an appropriate action for the SJB chief to submit an order he issued to the CSB?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some documents definitely had to be sent to the chief of the CSB, and I see that one of the recipients is the Banja Luka CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krgovic asked you some questions about police roadblocks or check-points that were near Keraterm, or possibly near Keraterm, on the morning following the room 3 killings. I want to show you P1009. Now, this is a dispatch from SJB Prijedor to CSB Banja Luka dated 24 July 1992. And we see it reports that due to well-known events in Prijedor, the police and military police have established mixed check-points at all entrances to and exits from the town of Prijedor, traversed by main roads. Now, you testified that you didn't encounter any check-points between Prijedor town and Keraterm camp that day, the day following the killings in room 3. But can you tell us whether there were any check-points that existed past Keraterm; in other words, further along the way to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we spoke about that day and I said that on our way in and out, or, rather, that there were no roadblock -- check-points on the day we came close to Keraterm. If that was the question. There were some check-points, as I said earlier today, but I myself didn't pass through them, and I don't know for what purpose they had been set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was marked for identification. May it be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there is -- I object to that. There is no nexus between -- because the witness never passed through the check-points. And, first of all, this line of question doesn't appear from my cross-examination. I asked precisely about the on-site investigation blocking the road nearby Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow, Mr. Olmsted, how you're seeking to tender this document through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, this witness has now established there were check-points. He didn't have to pass through them that day, but there were check-points, and he doesn't know why they existed. And this document does establish that these -- these check-points existed as well. And so it corroborates his testimony. It has already been marked for identification, and so we're simply seeking now to admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, the witness says there were some check-points. But this document obviously he doesn't know about. Why -- why should we take it in? We have the statement of the witness in. Why would we take it in with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I mean, other than calling the person who signed this, I don't think we're going to have another option as to a witness who can speak about check-points in and around the Prijedor area. And so this is really corroborating that issue as well as addressing the issue that Mr. Krgovic is trying to raise that there weren't such check-points existing around this time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I directly asked the witness about a previous testimony, that is to say, whether there was any roadblock before Keraterm and that traffic was stopped. And that was the only focus of my question. I didn't ask him about any other check-points in or out of Prijedor. And now we are talking at length here about some check-points that the witness had never gone through. So it has nothing to do with either my cross-examination or the response given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one sentence in support of Mr. Krgovic's objection: We have been repeatedly hearing from the OTP that they have no other witness through whom they can introduce this document. This is not a sufficient argument for introducing the document through any witness. They can be -- that can be done in a different way. We just shouldn't try and force the issue and admit this document into evidence through this witness. And I don't think that, what the Prosecutor says, that he doesn't have a proper witness, will suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: With respect, Mr. Cvijetic, I agree entirely with what you have just said. Mr. Olmsted, in our view, this document is not admissible. And it is time for the break, so we will adjourn and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if I may begin, could we have Exhibit P601 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, yesterday you had a chance to look at this document and answer some questions about it with -- from Mr. Krgovic. And it's a decision by the CSB chief establishing a commission. And as Mr. Krgovic explained and as we can see from the document itself, the commission had a significant number of tasks assigned to it, including visiting three municipalities, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi; establishing the existence of detention facilities in these three municipalities; determining why they were created, how they functioned; determining who was detained there and what conditions; and establishing whether the persons were leaving these three municipality, either voluntarily or by force. Now, we can see that the document is dated the 14th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the next page in the English but stay where we are in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that, towards the end of this document, that this -- that the commission's given until 1200 hours on 17 August 1992 to submit a report on these various issues. Mr. Rodic, based on your experience as a SDB officer, as well as your knowledge of the situation that existed in mid-August 1992, was three days sufficient time for a commission to interview everyone they needed to interview in order to provide a thorough analysis of all these issues?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the commission members used to gain this information, so I cannot be more specific about it. There are two or three days here; I don't know whether it was sufficient for them or not. I really cannot make any comments. And now as for what they used in order to put together this report, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During this time-period, August 1992, do you recall whether -- well, let me ask you this: Given the conditions of the roads and restrictions on travel in August 1992, how much time would it take to travel between Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Sanski Most? Could you do that in a day?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it -- it can -- it takes you half an hour to travel that distance. I don't know why it would take you a whole day. It's 30 kilometres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, transportation was free between those various locations at this time, August 1992? In other words, there was no reason to delay travelling between those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see any reason for any delays in that period. I don't see any reason why it would take a long time to travel from one point to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In this time-period, mid-August 1992, do you recall whether there was a lot of international media attention concerning the detention camps in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say anything about media attention. But there were some reports in our media, and I had no opportunity to follow any other media, to watch or to read any other media.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in response to a couple of Mr. Krgovic's questions yesterday and today, you mentioned that you were at Omarska camp for a couple of days towards the end of May of 1992. Can you tell us, what did you do while you were at Omarska camp during those couple of days?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I spent a day or two up there from the time when the investigation centre opened. We started performing some investigative measures. But this was a very short time-period, and I think that they went on doing that, up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, were you interviewing detainees while you were at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a day or two, I performed just a few interviews, minor stuff, because the work was just starting at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I believe it was suggested in your previous answer but it appears you didn't go alone. Did you go with other members of SDB and SJB to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't go there on my own. The colleagues who were with me in Keraterm and a number of colleagues who remained up there, working up there, they all went with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was Goran Novic amongst those that went with you to perform these interrogations?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was he one of the individuals who stayed at Omarska to continue on with interrogations after you returned to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, we thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. For the record, I'm Tom Hannis joining the Prosecution team. I have the next witness, ST-137. And if could I address a couple of procedural scheduling matters with you before we have him come in. First of all, I understand that the parties met earlier to discuss the issue of exhumations. My understanding: That those discussions were not fruitful and that it is a matter that we would like to address with you later in the week when we finish with the next two witnesses, whether that will be on Thursday or Friday, to discuss exhumations. And I think also some discussion about the Mladic materials and the parties' view on how we're going to proceed with dealing with those. The other matter I wanted to raise, and I'd like to go into private session, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Pursuant to the decision of the Trial Chamber of the 14th of July, 2010, in which it allowed the Prosecution to add 44 witnesses to the 65 ter list for the specific purpose of leading evidence to establish the substance of denied adjudicated facts, the Prosecution filed a notice and an addendum on the 22nd of July, 2010, in which it provided time estimates for the examination-in-chief of 23 viva voce witnesses from a total of 44, amounting to 47 hours and 15 minutes. The Trial Chamber, having assessed the scope of the testimony of each witness listed to testify viva voce and the relevant adjudicated facts, finds that 40 hours in total is sufficient for the examination-in-chief of the 23 identified witnesses. The Trial Chamber is also seized of the joint Defence motion seeking an order to compel the Prosecution to designate 92 bis and 92 quater packages for the 44 additional witness filed on the 4th of August. In the interest of efficient trial management, the Trial Chamber hereby orders the Prosecution to file the 92 bis and quater packages for the remaining 14 witnesses, whose testimony it proposes to adduce, in written form by Tuesday, the 28th of September, 2010. Thank you. The -- we would now go into closed session. The -- as -- as the next -- before we deal further with the intended witness.
